1. Introduction to Proposal
The Egmont Group (EG) has issued a Request for Proposals (RFP) seeking a secure and efficient data matching solution among Financial Intelligence Units (FIU) worldwide. In response, we propose a decentralized architecture leveraging modern, privacy-preserving data sharing technologies that maintain control, security, and scalability across FIU. Our solution provides encrypted data matching through the integration of Pando's data unification and search platform, which each FIU can install and manage, as well as an open source messaging system such as Apache Kafka to orchestrate the search requests between the private Pando applications, hosted on Azure or the FIU infrastructure.
With the use of our technology, FIU will experience fast, asynchronous data matching in line with the RFP’s requirements, removing the delays and human-error experienced today with a manual email approach.
We are confident our approach meets The EG’s listed requirements and further exceeds the requirements by offering encrypted distributed storage and search, encrypted search queries, and highly scalable solution.
2. About the Respondent - Pando
Pando is a private business located in Germany that specializes in building sophisticated entity resolution and search software for medium to large enterprise clients.
Our solutions are designed to help organizations integrate, deduplicate, and link disparate data sources to create unified, accurate views of entities such as individuals and organizations, and allow users to then search their unified datasets.
The founding team at Pando has advised and developed software for clients like the European Commission, including their fraud and anti-money laundering solution, Arachne. This platform enables European Union (EU) member state investigative units to upload data and use AI and machine learning, along with advanced search algorithms, to query global datasets—such as Moody's Orbis—to build a unified view of individuals and companies, which can then generate reports containing financial fraud alerts. 
The team has also consulted and developed a highly scalable entity resolution algorithm for Moody's Analytics datasets that scales to billions of records, allowing Moody’s teams to search entities across all their datasets.
All the systems we developed and designed have placed data security and privacy as the highest priority. We have also ensured that all users, such as EU member states, are treated equally, fostering an environment of mutual trust and fairness, in line with the RFP requirements. The EU Commission project took 6 months to develop the import, clean, standardize, and search features for this part of the project. We also managed to reduce the compute time for the batch search feature from days to minutes.
3. Proposed System Overview
   1. Pando suggested solution is a distributed encrypted search engine, where each FIU is treated equally by having their own Pando application which has their own backend database that is fully controlled and hosted by each FIU. The solution comprises the following key components to meet the requirements outlined in EG's RFP.
   2. Pando Search Application for Each FIU: Each FIU will host a custom solution based on our core tool, Pando, integrated into either its cloud or on-premises environment. You can check out a screenshot of the Pando UX, refer to Appendix B. The custom Pando solution connects to an FIU-specific database that serves as the backend to store sensitive entity data. Each database is independent and resides in the respective FIU Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) environment, ensuring that each unit's data sovereignty is respected and maintained.
The custom Pando solution serves as the user interface for all users within an FIU, managing user accounts and permissions using existing Identity and Access Management (IAM) solutions. It allows each user to perform searches and upload documents. During document uploads, the custom Pando solution will clean, standardize, transliterate, and perform entity extraction before encrypting and storing the data inside Elasticsearch. Elasticsearch can scale to billions of records with response times of 0.001 sec per query. The FIU user will have full control over what data can and can't be used when other FIU search against it.
   3. Centralized Search Coordination Using Apache Kafka: Our architecture includes a central Kafka cluster that acts as a Search Board for encrypted queries between FIU. You can check out the system design in the Appendix A. Kafka serves as a scalable, open-source messaging broker that is highly reliable for distributing encrypted search requests and responses. FIU can submit encrypted search queries to the Kafka Search Board, which allows each FIU Pando application to read the submitted queries and process them asynchronously, then send back the responses. This approach provides an extra line of security, as Pando applications do not need direct internet connectivity and can be deployed in private subnets that read from the Kafka Search Board.
   4. Encrypted Communication and Data Storage: Data security is of utmost importance in our solution. All data within the Elasticsearch databases, as well as the search queries, are encrypted with strong cryptographic keys managed by each FIU. This end-to-end encryption model ensures that data remains unreadable in transit and at rest, minimizing security vulnerabilities.
   5. Privacy-Preserving Search: Data matching across FIU occurs by means of a privacy-preserving mechanism based on private set intersection (PSI). This approach ensures that FIU can identify matches without sharing sensitive data directly. Each FIU Pando application reads from the kafka query board and gets the encrypted search requests and conducts searches within its own Elasticsearch database. Only relevant results are returned to the querying FIU, maintaining the privacy of other non-matching entities.
   6. Automation for Follow-Up Processes: Pando will include a feature to automate follow-up processes after a possible hit. This feature will include notifying relevant parties, triggering investigations, and initiating collaborative workflows for international cooperation using systems already built by EG, such as the multilateral information exchange system (ESW). 
   4. Implementation Details
   1. Data Storage: All FIU will use Elasticsearch instances to store data. Each instance is isolated, encrypted, and accessible only within the VPC of each FIU, thus providing a robust data sovereignty guarantee.
   2. Encrypted Search Requests: The Kafka Search Board is responsible for managing encrypted search requests and responses among the FIU. This component ensures that no plaintext data is exposed during the search operation. The encryption is managed via an encryption key shared among participating FIU.
   3. Scalable and Fault-Tolerant Design: Both Elasticsearch and Kafka are designed to be fault-tolerant and highly scalable, supporting the addition of new FIU without impacting the existing architecture. This modularity enables EG to onboard new members seamlessly.
   4. Compliance and Security: Our solution adheres to industry standards in data security and privacy. By leveraging encryption, VPC isolation, and strong access control measures, we can guarantee that all data transfers and storage comply with data protection laws and international regulations.
   5. On Going Support and Training: 
   1. Initial Training & Onboarding: Training for FIU staff during setup, including user guides and video tutorials.
   2. Dedicated Support: 24/7 email and phone support with a dedicated representative for critical issues.
   3. Feature Updates: Regular training sessions on new features and release notes for system changes.
   4. Workshops & Customization: Periodic workshops for advanced users and customization support to adapt workflows and system features.
   5. Knowledge Sharing: Access to a user community for sharing experiences and best practices among FIU. 
   5. Functional Requirements
   1. All FIU should be treated equally. The solution must be implementable in FIU with very diverse IT environments and different security policies. 
We meet this requirement by providing each FIU with their own Pando application, which can be installed as a Docker container or private web app inside the FIU cloud environment whose only requirement is outgoing internet access to the central kafka broker.
   2. Security is key and is more important than usability / user friendliness of the IT solution.
We meet this requirement by ensuring that all communications and data within our solution are encrypted at all stages, both in transit and at rest, using strong cryptographic keys managed by each FIU. Additionally, our use of private set intersection and isolated VPC deployment prioritizes security over ease of use, providing the most secure environment possible while still enabling effective data matching.
   3. Only intended recipients of any communication can access the content. No third party, including service providers, administrators, or other bodies might have access. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring that all data and communication within our solution are encrypted with keys unique to each FIU, which are never shared with third parties. We use end-to-end encryption mechanisms to guarantee that no one outside of the intended recipient, including service providers, administrators, or intermediaries, has any access to the content.
   4. The solution should not require excessive efforts for FIU to implement and actively use the solution. 
We meet this requirement by providing an easy-to-deploy Pando application that can be installed as either a Docker container, kubernetes service, virtual machine images and or terraform code. This allows FIU to set up the system quickly with minimal IT overhead.
   5. The IT solution should be future-proof and be able to include future EG requirements.
We meet this requirement by designing the Pando application as a modular and extensible system. This means future features or requirements, such as new data types, enhanced analytics, or additional privacy controls, can be easily integrated without significant modifications to the existing system.
   6. The solution shall enable FIU to identify hits between subjects of interest to one FIU and those of another, without revealing the list of queried subjects to the other FIU 
We meet this requirement by using a privacy-preserving technique called Private Set Intersection (PSI). PSI allows FIU to identify matches between their subjects of interest without sharing the actual list of queried subjects. Each FIU Pando application processes encrypted queries, and only the matched results are returned to the querying FIU, ensuring that non-matching data remains private.
   7. The solution shall enable FIU to make essential information available for the matching without sharing sensitive data
We meet this requirement by ensuring that our privacy-preserving approach uses encryption and private set intersection techniques. Each FIU retains control of sensitive data, only sharing essential and encrypted information for matching, ensuring privacy at all times.
   8. The solution shall enable FIU to be in full control of which data is used in such sharing processes.
We meet this requirement by allowing each FIU to determine exactly what data can be shared and under which conditions. The Pando application gives FIU granular control over data permissions, ensuring they have full autonomy over the use of their data in any sharing or matching processes.
   9. The solution shall enable FIU to share within limited groups of users. 
We meet this requirement by allowing each FIU to set specific data-sharing permissions that define which groups of users can access particular datasets. The Pando application includes configurable access control features, enabling FIU to limit data sharing within specific user groups.
   10. The solution shall enable FIU to facilitate follow-up processes to validate possible matches and initiate bilateral and/or multilateral information exchange using ESW.
We meet this requirement by allowing Pando to easily integrate with tools to facilitate the follow-up procedure.
   11. The solution shall limit the decision if and to what degree FIU use matching remains with the FIU only. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring that each FIU has complete autonomy over whether and how they use the matching functionality, maintaining full control over their participation.
   12. The solution shall limit data transformation and matching are local processes. Only transformed data can leave the source. All non-transformed data remains at the source. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring that all data transformations and matching computations are performed locally, with only the transformed results being shared externally.
   13. The solution should be built on a privacy-by-design approach. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring that privacy is integrated at every stage of the system design, including data encryption, access control, and secure data sharing mechanisms.
   14. The solution must use the current technical framework, especially the security design and Identity and Access management elements. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring the Pando application can fully integrate with existing security infrastructure and IAM systems, allowing seamless compatibility and adherence to established security protocols.
   15. A decentralized approach to foster data security should be at least optional. 
We meet this requirement by providing the option for each FIU to run its own Pando instance independently, ensuring data is stored locally and reducing the risk of centralized data breaches.
   16. Automation should be supported for follow-up processes after a possible hit, fostering efficient processes for international collaboration. 
We meet this requirement by ensuring the Pando application can fully integrate automation features that support notifications, investigations, and collaboration tools to streamline international follow-up processes.

On 15th October, 2017, 51 representatives (of a possible 183) from the Austrian Freedom Party (Freiheitliche Partei Österreichs, or FPÖ) were elected to the Nationalrat, the Austrian national parliament. This left the FPÖ—under the leadership of Heinz-Christian Strache—as the third largest party in the Austrian parliament, holding only one seat fewer than the very well established Austrian Social Democratic Party (Sozialdemokratische Partei Österreichs). The success of the FPÖ follows two trends: first, the revival of far-right nationalist political forces globally from 2016 onwards; second, the turn to the far-right in Austria in light of high migrant influxes. In other words, the outcome of the 2017 Nationalratswahl (parliamentary election) was at - at least to some degree - predictable. In this article I intend on comparing the Freedom Party’s rise to power in the 1990s and in 2017, as well as analyse how the FPÖ was able to draw upon the sentiments of disgruntled and out-of-pocket Austrians to make Old Boys clubs in vogue again in the 21st century.


Far-right politics has been more visible in Austria over the last three decades than in many other advanced European democracies. Most notably in neighbouring Germany the rise of the Alternative for Germany has been a very recent phenomenon. The FPÖ’s share of the vote has been gradually increasing since the 2002 Nationalratswahl. This trend that culminated in the second biggest electoral success in the FPÖ’s history certainly emphasises that the voter base of this party is different to those of other populist forces, whose support amongst the electorate grew only several years after the 2008 financial crisis. From this we can conclude, then, that the FPÖ’s success cannot simply by viewed as adherent to the post-2008 pan-European lurch to the political right. Instead, far-right politics in Austria enjoys support from a relatively consistent group of voters.


It is important to remember at this point that in 1999 the Freedom Party of Austria was able to secure 52 seats in the Nationalrat — the party’s biggest electoral haul. Much like the 2017 result, this victory for far-right politics was the end product of 14 years of consistent improvement at the polls. The Freedom Party—led at that time by the controversial Jörg Haider—was able to capitalise on a variety of different sentiments during this period. In pre-2000 Austria such sentiments were in part brought on by growing numbers of migrants from former Soviet Union and Yugoslavian nations. However, Thomas Fillitz argues that the FPÖ’s primary success came from the party’s call for democratisation—in terms of both challenging the hegemony of the two-party system and pushing for direct democracy through referenda. In short, it was a combination of direct democracy and xenophobia that allowed the Freedom Party to thrive—a combination that may sound all too familiar to Brexit-beleaguered Britain.


Though many on the left and in the centre may be reluctant to praise a party whose former leader made allusions to positive aspects of the Nazi times, we must accept that any party able to not only break the established political mould, but also force mainstream parties to reengage with the electorate is bringing out the best in democracy.


It was a political spat between Haider and other party members during the 1999 coalition that drove the FPÖ to split and eventually reimagine itself under Strache’s guidance. This schism weakened the party’s electoral presence in the 2002 Nationalratswahl (parliamentary election). But the electorate did not take long to warm to the FPÖ once again. In the following four elections the party was able to increase its share of the vote from 11% to 26%. And voilà, by 2017 the Freedom Party was once more the junior coalition partner of the Social Democrats with 51 seats in the Austrian parliament. In the blink of twenty years the far-right are back with a bang.


It does not take a political scientist (and I do not claim to be one) to tell you that the FPÖ’s first  recipe (democracy + xenophobia) for success has become ubiquitous for far-right European parties in the post-2008 political landscape. Whether it’s kartulisalat-munching electorate in Estonia, the seduced-by-Salvini Italians or the boggled-by-Brexit Brits, the European electorate has developed a taste for xenophobic politics seasoned (often heavily) with claims of re-democratisation. Even across the pond, Donald Trump has taken to serving his supporters a toxic spew of anti-migrant rhetoric coupled with ‘anti-system’ narratives.


It is only fair that we view the current success of the FPÖ in the context of this global lurch to the right. Yet, where previously the Freedom Party was able to genuinely shake up the order of things in Austria —and in this sense fulfil its pre-election promises— now the party is simply riding the populist wave. This populist wave is most probably the result of what the Stanford political scientist Francis Fukuyama calls identity politics. In his book Identity Politics Fukuyama discusses the death of class-based politics on the left, with equal respect, dignity and recognition of every citizen’s internal self being prioritised over economic equality. Middle-class liberals who have been least affected by growing wealth disparity in western nations do not share as many economic concerns as those in the working class and thus prioritise civil and legal equality. Thus, those feeling the pinch of post-industrialised economies — the working class — can no longer turn to the left to fight their battles for them. So they turn to the right instead.


Right wing identity politics requires a collective body of people who share a coherent cultural identity, Fukuyama argues. This body of people gazes longingly to a better past where this perceived cultural identity was the norm. Such nostalgic longings for a society of the past where community appeared strong are a symptom of an electorate disenfranchised by the processes of globalisation. Austria—like all other western countries—was hit hard by the 2008 crisis. Sparpolitik (austerity) induced by lack of available government in the post-2008 economic landscape has accentuated the gap between those reliant on public services and those who aren’t. Furthermore, job automation and outsourcing have left the lowest skilled members of the work force either unemployed or in dead-end tertiary sector roles.


While economic dissatisfaction is certainly the catalyst for the formation of far-right collective identities, it would be misguided to suggest that it is the singular root cause of the electoral success enjoyed by the FPÖ in 2017. Official figures state that number of documented migrants from Asia (which includes Iraq, Iran and Syria) has nearly tripled in the last nine years, and that the number of African migrants grew by around 75% percent over the same period. Such considerable influxes of largely Muslim migrants into Austria have served as a perfect outlet for an already disgruntled working class.


Islamic identities present not only a racial Other for the largely white Christian population of Austria. They also create a moral paradox for liberals and elites. On the one hand, liberal-left political identities dictate that new migrant arrivées should be granted equal dignity and respect for their inner identities. On the other, this entails advocating for and defending the exercising of Islamic identities, which—especially considering the previous societies in which migrants lived—do not grant such equality to many social groups, women and the LGBTQ+ community to name two.


This could either be a contradictory position to take, or an obsessively liberal one. However, it is the criticism that liberals level at their white, Christian compatriots for calling out issues with Islamic conservatism which cements this aspect of liberal logic as partially flawed, if not contradictory. This is not to say that FPÖ supporters are not guilty of espousing xenophobia towards and holding heavily prejudiced views against Muslim migrants. But such misguided views much be challenged with the same urgency as those ultra-conservative views held by some in the Muslim migrant community. As this has not happened, and as the liberal order has yet to come up with convincing economic reforms that will result in either a perceived or actual change in wealth inequality, populist parties will continue to be a driving force in western politics irrespective of their questionable motivations.


Since forming a coalition in 2017, the SPÖ-FPÖ coalition has failed to spur on any significant economic growth in Austria. In 2018 imports and exports grew by 5.5% and 5.4%, respectively. In 2017, however, both these figures were around 4% higher. 2018 domestic retail sales grew 50% less than they did in 2017. And Austria’s GDP growth falls pretty much in to line with the rest of the stagnant Eurozone. It is clear that Freedom Party’s approach to economics—basic free market principles, low tax rates and sufficient social welfare—is failing to produce any admirable level of economic growth. Such uninspiring figures mean that the FPÖ will have to rely on a war of words to convince voters of its commitment to the Heimat (homeland).


Unfortunately, the Freedom Party’s love to Heimat takes an uncomfortably racist form. The Freedom Party was a chief sponsor of the 2019 Burschenbundball (Fraternity Ball) in Austria’s third largest city, Linz. This exclusive event is attended by elitist social networks somewhat similar to, though slightly less classist than, the Bullingdon Club in the UK. As reported in Vice, the FPÖ appeared on the front page of the sponsor booklet. A grinning Christian-Heinz Strache reassures attendees that its okay to say Ja zum Vaterland! (Yes to the Fatherland!). In addition to these semantic links to the Nazi-era, the Burschenbundball plays host to an array of ethnonationalist ‘fraternities’. The first of these is the so-called Identitäre Bewegung, which advocates ethnopluralism (societies divided by race). The second is Teutonia. The name refers to a nomadic German tribe documented by the Romans. Teutonia was embroiled in a scandal when it was discovered that frat members used the Ostmark when referring to Austria in writing. The Ostmark was a symbol made popular by the Nazis during post-Anschluss (annexation) Austria. If that wasn’t enough, the sponsor booklet was littered with Kornblume, a blue flower used by Austrian Nazis as a secret symbol to identify themselves to other Nazis. Finally, the booklet contained song lyrics from SS troop songs. All this together means that the junior coalition partner of the Austrian government fosters ethnonationalists and neo-nazis. We really have to ask: how can the liberal left still be losing this battle?


Beyond propagating anti-semitic signs and symbols, Burschengemeinschaften (fraternities) serve as an Old Boys club. Though, of course, open to women, such organisations are not egalitarian in their nature. Membership to such clubs also gets you access to jobs—employers can advertise positions directly on frat website. As we have seen above, memberships can only (really) be extended to white Christians. And while this includes the majority of Austrians, most people do not (and rightly so) want to be a part of this misogynistic and racist club. Thus, the networking and employment opportunities provided by Burschengemeinschaften remain available to only a select few. 


From all of this we can draw the following conclusions about the Austrian Freedom Party. Firstly, there are genuine xenophobic drivers within the party, which allows it to connect personally with many voters who harbour racist or islamophobic opinions and views (right wing identity politics). This is an authentic relationship which builds trust-- something centrist politicians seriously lack. In turn, this enables voters to ignore the party’s economic policies, which effectively seek no serious change in either wealth redistribution or power relations in Austria. In other words, wealth inequality — one of the other key drivers of populist politics — will not change. Secondly, today’s Freedom Party has done little to improve the standing of democracy in Austria like it did under its previous leadership. Cooperating with anti-democratic actors such as Vladimir Putin is, in fact, an example of the party damaging democracy. Instead, we have seen how populism has —again— become a vehicle for self-enrichment of those who were dealt a good hand in life. Finally, we must accept that class politics is well and truly dead. A collective identity based in xenophobia shared by members of both exclusionary fraternities and a struggling working class has trumped the diverging economic interests between them.

Hailing from Southeast Asia, this popular elephant's ear (Alocasia amazonica, part
of the Alocasia genus) is sometimes called African Mask. It's a hybrid that has
become a fairly popular ornamental houseplant and is one of the easiest to find
and buy. A striking and beautiful houseplant, it is defined by its deep green leaves
accentuated by whitish or light green veins. The leaves are roughly serrated, and in
some cases, the leaf color appears as an almost purple-green. Leaf shapes range
from wide hearts to slim arrowheads, with textures from slick and glossy to thick
and waxy. It is a fleshy evergreen that grows from underground corms. These plants
rarely bloom, however, and are grown primarily for their foliage.
How to Grow Amazon Elephant's Ear
Amazon elephant ears are striking, with dramatic and unique two-tone leaf
coloration. Growing elephant ears is easy—they like filtered sun or shade and rich,
moist soil—and they grow rapidly. A large specimen may grow up to 3 feet but most
are smaller. Like most tropical plants, they thrive in warm temperatures and high
humidity and crave plenty of water. Cut away dead and dying leaves for the best
presentation, and keep an eye out for mites.

Light
These plants require bright, indirect light. They can survive in 80 percent shade but
prefer about 60 percent shade. Do not expose to strong, direct sunlight.
Water
Keep the soil moist but remember that Alocasias do not like wet feet. If possible,
water in the morning (so they are dry overnight) and from below, at the root zone,
to keep the leaves from getting too wet. This plant needs a rest period in winter
when you should allow the soil to become almost dry between waterings and stop
fertilizing. If it dries completely it may go dormant, but if it does you may be able to
dig up the corm and save it until warmer conditions are possible.
Temperature and Humidity
Being a tropical plant, Amazon elephant's ear will go dormant or die if exposed to
cold. It likes to be in a climate similar to its native Southeast Asia: a temperature
between 65 F and 75 Fahrenheit and above-average humidity is ideal. You may need
to raise the humidity levels in a room artificially by placing the plant in a humidity
tray with pebbles or use a humidifier.
Soil
This plant prefers a fast-draining, well-aerated potting soil. An organic, loose soil
that contains a good amount of peat moss is ideal. If needed, add some builder's
sand or Perlite to lighten a heavier soil.
Fertilizer
Amazon elephant's ear tends to be a heavy feeder during its growing period and will
respond well to applications of diluted balanced fertilizer. Starting in spring, feed
the plant every two weeks. Stop the end of August, then start the cycle again at
the beginning of the next spring. Occasionally, the leaves will yellow; if this
happens, try adding fertilizer with micronutrients or sprinkle Epsom salts around
the base of the plant once a month.

On 15th October, 2017, 51 representatives (of a possible 183) from the Austrian Freedom Party (Freiheitliche Partei Österreichs, or FPÖ) were elected to the Nationalrat, the Austrian national parliament. This left the FPÖ—under the leadership of Heinz-Christian Strache—as the third largest party in the Austrian parliament, holding only one seat fewer than the very well established Austrian Social Democratic Party (Sozialdemokratische Partei Österreichs). The success of the FPÖ follows two trends: first, the revival of far-right nationalist political forces globally from 2016 onwards; second, the turn to the far-right in Austria in light of high migrant influxes. In other words, the outcome of the 2017 Nationalratswahl (parliamentary election) was at - at least to some degree - predictable. In this article I intend on comparing the Freedom Party’s rise to power in the 1990s and in 2017, as well as analyse how the FPÖ was able to draw upon the sentiments of disgruntled and out-of-pocket Austrians to make Old Boys clubs in vogue again in the 21st century.


Far-right politics has been more visible in Austria over the last three decades than in many other advanced European democracies. Most notably in neighbouring Germany the rise of the Alternative for Germany has been a very recent phenomenon. The FPÖ’s share of the vote has been gradually increasing since the 2002 Nationalratswahl. This trend that culminated in the second biggest electoral success in the FPÖ’s history certainly emphasises that the voter base of this party is different to those of other populist forces, whose support amongst the electorate grew only several years after the 2008 financial crisis. From this we can conclude, then, that the FPÖ’s success cannot simply by viewed as adherent to the post-2008 pan-European lurch to the political right. Instead, far-right politics in Austria enjoys support from a relatively consistent group of voters.


It is important to remember at this point that in 1999 the Freedom Party of Austria was able to secure 52 seats in the Nationalrat — the party’s biggest electoral haul. Much like the 2017 result, this victory for far-right politics was the end product of 14 years of consistent improvement at the polls. The Freedom Party—led at that time by the controversial Jörg Haider—was able to capitalise on a variety of different sentiments during this period. In pre-2000 Austria such sentiments were in part brought on by growing numbers of migrants from former Soviet Union and Yugoslavian nations. However, Thomas Fillitz argues that the FPÖ’s primary success came from the party’s call for democratisation—in terms of both challenging the hegemony of the two-party system and pushing for direct democracy through referenda. In short, it was a combination of direct democracy and xenophobia that allowed the Freedom Party to thrive—a combination that may sound all too familiar to Brexit-beleaguered Britain.


Though many on the left and in the centre may be reluctant to praise a party whose former leader made allusions to positive aspects of the Nazi times, we must accept that any party able to not only break the established political mould, but also force mainstream parties to reengage with the electorate is bringing out the best in democracy.


It was a political spat between Haider and other party members during the 1999 coalition that drove the FPÖ to split and eventually reimagine itself under Strache’s guidance. This schism weakened the party’s electoral presence in the 2002 Nationalratswahl (parliamentary election). But the electorate did not take long to warm to the FPÖ once again. In the following four elections the party was able to increase its share of the vote from 11% to 26%. And voilà, by 2017 the Freedom Party was once more the junior coalition partner of the Social Democrats with 51 seats in the Austrian parliament. In the blink of twenty years the far-right are back with a bang.


It does not take a political scientist (and I do not claim to be one) to tell you that the FPÖ’s first  recipe (democracy + xenophobia) for success has become ubiquitous for far-right European parties in the post-2008 political landscape. Whether it’s kartulisalat-munching electorate in Estonia, the seduced-by-Salvini Italians or the boggled-by-Brexit Brits, the European electorate has developed a taste for xenophobic politics seasoned (often heavily) with claims of re-democratisation. Even across the pond, Donald Trump has taken to serving his supporters a toxic spew of anti-migrant rhetoric coupled with ‘anti-system’ narratives.


It is only fair that we view the current success of the FPÖ in the context of this global lurch to the right. Yet, where previously the Freedom Party was able to genuinely shake up the order of things in Austria —and in this sense fulfil its pre-election promises— now the party is simply riding the populist wave. This populist wave is most probably the result of what the Stanford political scientist Francis Fukuyama calls identity politics. In his book Identity Politics Fukuyama discusses the death of class-based politics on the left, with equal respect, dignity and recognition of every citizen’s internal self being prioritised over economic equality. Middle-class liberals who have been least affected by growing wealth disparity in western nations do not share as many economic concerns as those in the working class and thus prioritise civil and legal equality. Thus, those feeling the pinch of post-industrialised economies — the working class — can no longer turn to the left to fight their battles for them. So they turn to the right instead.


Right wing identity politics requires a collective body of people who share a coherent cultural identity, Fukuyama argues. This body of people gazes longingly to a better past where this perceived cultural identity was the norm. Such nostalgic longings for a society of the past where community appeared strong are a symptom of an electorate disenfranchised by the processes of globalisation. Austria—like all other western countries—was hit hard by the 2008 crisis. Sparpolitik (austerity) induced by lack of available government in the post-2008 economic landscape has accentuated the gap between those reliant on public services and those who aren’t. Furthermore, job automation and outsourcing have left the lowest skilled members of the work force either unemployed or in dead-end tertiary sector roles.


While economic dissatisfaction is certainly the catalyst for the formation of far-right collective identities, it would be misguided to suggest that it is the singular root cause of the electoral success enjoyed by the FPÖ in 2017. Official figures state that number of documented migrants from Asia (which includes Iraq, Iran and Syria) has nearly tripled in the last nine years, and that the number of African migrants grew by around 75% percent over the same period. Such considerable influxes of largely Muslim migrants into Austria have served as a perfect outlet for an already disgruntled working class.


Islamic identities present not only a racial Other for the largely white Christian population of Austria. They also create a moral paradox for liberals and elites. On the one hand, liberal-left political identities dictate that new migrant arrivées should be granted equal dignity and respect for their inner identities. On the other, this entails advocating for and defending the exercising of Islamic identities, which—especially considering the previous societies in which migrants lived—do not grant such equality to many social groups, women and the LGBTQ+ community to name two.


This could either be a contradictory position to take, or an obsessively liberal one. However, it is the criticism that liberals level at their white, Christian compatriots for calling out issues with Islamic conservatism which cements this aspect of liberal logic as partially flawed, if not contradictory. This is not to say that FPÖ supporters are not guilty of espousing xenophobia towards and holding heavily prejudiced views against Muslim migrants. But such misguided views much be challenged with the same urgency as those ultra-conservative views held by some in the Muslim migrant community. As this has not happened, and as the liberal order has yet to come up with convincing economic reforms that will result in either a perceived or actual change in wealth inequality, populist parties will continue to be a driving force in western politics irrespective of their questionable motivations.


Since forming a coalition in 2017, the SPÖ-FPÖ coalition has failed to spur on any significant economic growth in Austria. In 2018 imports and exports grew by 5.5% and 5.4%, respectively. In 2017, however, both these figures were around 4% higher. 2018 domestic retail sales grew 50% less than they did in 2017. And Austria’s GDP growth falls pretty much in to line with the rest of the stagnant Eurozone. It is clear that Freedom Party’s approach to economics—basic free market principles, low tax rates and sufficient social welfare—is failing to produce any admirable level of economic growth. Such uninspiring figures mean that the FPÖ will have to rely on a war of words to convince voters of its commitment to the Heimat (homeland).


Unfortunately, the Freedom Party’s love to Heimat takes an uncomfortably racist form. The Freedom Party was a chief sponsor of the 2019 Burschenbundball (Fraternity Ball) in Austria’s third largest city, Linz. This exclusive event is attended by elitist social networks somewhat similar to, though slightly less classist than, the Bullingdon Club in the UK. As reported in Vice, the FPÖ appeared on the front page of the sponsor booklet. A grinning Christian-Heinz Strache reassures attendees that its okay to say Ja zum Vaterland! (Yes to the Fatherland!). In addition to these semantic links to the Nazi-era, the Burschenbundball plays host to an array of ethnonationalist ‘fraternities’. The first of these is the so-called Identitäre Bewegung, which advocates ethnopluralism (societies divided by race). The second is Teutonia. The name refers to a nomadic German tribe documented by the Romans. Teutonia was embroiled in a scandal when it was discovered that frat members used the Ostmark when referring to Austria in writing. The Ostmark was a symbol made popular by the Nazis during post-Anschluss (annexation) Austria. If that wasn’t enough, the sponsor booklet was littered with Kornblume, a blue flower used by Austrian Nazis as a secret symbol to identify themselves to other Nazis. Finally, the booklet contained song lyrics from SS troop songs. All this together means that the junior coalition partner of the Austrian government fosters ethnonationalists and neo-nazis. We really have to ask: how can the liberal left still be losing this battle?


Beyond propagating anti-semitic signs and symbols, Burschengemeinschaften (fraternities) serve as an Old Boys club. Though, of course, open to women, such organisations are not egalitarian in their nature. Membership to such clubs also gets you access to jobs—employers can advertise positions directly on frat website. As we have seen above, memberships can only (really) be extended to white Christians. And while this includes the majority of Austrians, most people do not (and rightly so) want to be a part of this misogynistic and racist club. Thus, the networking and employment opportunities provided by Burschengemeinschaften remain available to only a select few. 


From all of this we can draw the following conclusions about the Austrian Freedom Party. Firstly, there are genuine xenophobic drivers within the party, which allows it to connect personally with many voters who harbour racist or islamophobic opinions and views (right wing identity politics). This is an authentic relationship which builds trust-- something centrist politicians seriously lack. In turn, this enables voters to ignore the party’s economic policies, which effectively seek no serious change in either wealth redistribution or power relations in Austria. In other words, wealth inequality — one of the other key drivers of populist politics — will not change. Secondly, today’s Freedom Party has done little to improve the standing of democracy in Austria like it did under its previous leadership. Cooperating with anti-democratic actors such as Vladimir Putin is, in fact, an example of the party damaging democracy. Instead, we have seen how populism has —again— become a vehicle for self-enrichment of those who were dealt a good hand in life. Finally, we must accept that class politics is well and truly dead. Identity politics, as Francis Fukuyama understands it, now rules victorious. A collective identity based in xenophobia shared by members of both exclusionary fraternities and a struggling working class has trumped the diverging economic interests between them. 


To find a solution to this issue, centrists must be willing to radically reform certain areas of the economy. A relevelling of the economic playing field will regain trust in voters who see the centre as morally contradictory and ‘in the pockets’ of the global elite. Similarly, liberals have to accept that rapid demographic changes negatively affect social cohesion. Wealth distribution can negate this, but migration policy must be reexamined. Though FPÖ voters’ claims about liberal ‘elites’ contain elements of truth, populists have nothing in the way of innovative economic solutions.
